Article Title: As riding costs hurt, Tesla tells employees: You cannot spend more than $200 on…
Article Text:
From ‘use more AI’ to ‘please, use less’



The carve-out that points straight to xAI



Why the bill matters more than usual for Tesla



Tesla has told its staff to stop burning cash on artificial intelligence. Starting July 6, employees can spend no more than $200 a week on AI tools, according to an internal memo first reported by The Information. The cap arrives just months after Tesla was pushing workers to use AI as hard as they could—a whiplash turn that says a lot about where the AI spending boom is heading.Anyone who wants to go past the $200 line now needs sign-off. Before the limit, some software engineers were reportedly chewing through thousands of dollars in tokens every week. Tokens are the units that measure AI usage, and every prompt eats into the bill.The reversal is fast even by Tesla standards. Over the past six months, the company moved scattered AI use onto a single approved platform called Bottle Rocket, stocked with models from OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Cursor. Some teams built dashboards that ranked employees by how many tokens they consumed, nudging everyone to use more.It worked too well. The heaviest users ran up weekly bills in the thousands, and now the same company that gamified consumption is slamming on the brakes.Here's the detail that gives the game away. The $200 cap does not apply to beta versions of xAI products—Elon Musk's own AI company. So the policy quietly steers heavy users toward Grok and Cursor's Composer model rather than rivals.Musk has spent months nudging Tesla staff toward tools tied to his other ventures. He emailed the whole company urging people to try Composer after his AI lab started working with Cursor. SpaceX is now set to buy Cursor's parent, Anysphere, for $60 billion.The push isn't landing. Grok is unpopular inside Tesla, and many engineers reach for Anthropic's Claude instead, according to people familiar with the matter. When you need a spending limit to win internal users for your own product, that's not a vote of confidence.Tesla's whole valuation now rests on AI. Musk has said the company's future depends on deploying it across the Robotaxi network and the Optimus humanoid robot, not on selling cars—and revenue has been roughly flat for two years. That makes the spending story awkward. If Tesla can't manage a few thousand dollars of weekly token spend per engineer, questions about scaling AI across a robotaxi fleet and millions of robots are fair game.The move mirrors a wider corporate retreat from "tokenmaxxing," the trend of measuring AI productivity by sheer usage. Uber capped spending at $1,500 a month after blowing through its entire 2026 AI budget by April. Meta, Amazon, and Walmart have all rolled out caps or steered staff toward cheaper models as token-based billing exposed them to the true cost of every prompt.Tesla has been tightening on security too, restricting access to models outside Bottle Rocket on company machines and warning staff not to feed confidential data into unapproved systems. For now, the message to Tesla's engineers is simple: the free-spending phase is over, and the meter is running.
Article Summary: Tesla has told its staff to stop burning cash on artificial intelligence. Starting July 6, employees can spend no more than $200 a week on AI tools. The cap arrives just months after Tesla was pushing workers to use AI as hard as they could. The heaviest users ran up weekly bills in the thousands.

Article Title: 17,625 tablets in 64 hours: China's Agibot completes world's first livestream of humanoid robots inspecting production line with 99% accuracy
Article Text:
Image credit: X

Livestream focused on industrial manufacturing



“By bringing multiple humanoid robots into a real production line and making the process visible over six consecutive days, we wanted to provide a more transparent answer to what embodied AI industrialisation actually requires,”

China-based robotics company Agibot has completed what Chinese state media described as the world's first livestream of humanoid robots operating across a full tablet production inspection line. The six-day demonstration, which concluded recently after eight humanoid robots worked on an active manufacturing line at Longcheer Technology's factory in Nanchang, produced 17,625 tablets while achieving a reported task success rate of 99.99%.During the livestream, the robots ran for more than 64 hours of runtime, nonstop in a commercial factory environment, the People’s Daily China said in a post on X. The demonstration was live-streamed to the public, showing the robots performing manufacturing tasks in a normal production environment.The robots, identified as Agibot's G2 humanoid models, handled tablet inspection, defect sorting, material transport and other production activities across more than four manufacturing workflows. Agibot said the robots completed 64,828 production-line tasks during the demonstration while working alongside human employees and active industrial equipment.Unlike in controlled laboratory demonstrations, the robots operated on a functioning mass-production line, adapting to changing production requirements in real time.According to the company, the livestream was intended to demonstrate the use of humanoid robots in practical industrial environments through continuous public observation over six days.said Yao Maoqing, president of Embodied AI Business Unit at AGIBOT, in a statement.Following the livestream, Agibot announced that its 15,000th robot had rolled off its production line and been delivered to its manufacturing partner, Longcheer.The milestone robot is an Agibot G2, a wheeled mobile manipulator with a humanoid upper body designed for industrial tasks including material handling, inspection and production-line support. The company said it has accelerated production over the past year, reducing the time to increase cumulative output from 5,000 to 10,000 robots to three months, down from about a year to scale from 1,000 to 5,000 units.The livestream comes months after Figure AI completed a 200-hour autonomous livestream featuring its Figure 03 humanoid robots, which the company said processed nearly 250,000 packages without a hardware failure.
Article Summary: Livestream focused on industrial manufacturing in Nanchang, China. Eight humanoid robots produced 17,625 tablets while achieving a reported task success rate of 99.99%. The demonstration was live-streamed to the public, showing the robots performing manufacturing tasks in a normal production environment.

Article Title: Millionaire Bryan Johnson opens up about autoimmune disease damaging his stomach, says ‘Hard to detect, often silent’
Article Text:
Bryan Johnson

Read Bryan Johnson’s complete post here



Post by Bryan Johnson Bad news #1:

I have an autoimmune disease. My stomach is eating itself.

Bad news #2:

2–5% of people have this, too. Likely more, because it hides.

Good news:

I'm going to try and solve it. Will share all.

As a kid, I ate sugar cereal, drank sugary soda, and gobbled down fast food. I had a few healthy years in my early 20s but then became a young father of three and began building a business.

Juggling that stress and grind, I let my health slip and gained 40 lbs. Within a few years I’d fallen into a deep, chronic depression.

Somewhere in that timeline, my body began developing an autoimmune process affecting my thyroid and then my stomach lining.

It’s called Autoimmune Gastritis (AIG).

My hypothyroidism got diagnosed when I was 21 years old with a routine blood draw. That enabled me to begin proactive management, supplementing levothyroxine and Armour Thyroid. They are the hormones my body should be producing on its own but wasn’t.

By taking these pills daily, my body was able to operate as though my thyroid was functioning properly. What I didn’t know was that something else was going on inside my body: my stomach had begun attacking itself. But there was no routine test to find out and I didn’t have any symptoms.

I just discovered it in May. I'm unsure how long I've had it. AIG causes irreversible damage: nutritional deficiency, anemia, and over a long horizon, elevated cancer risk. When AIG is discovered today, standard medical care concedes defeat, stating that nothing can be done except managing the condition, no matter how awful or lethal the effects.

Looking back over the past few years, I can now see the early signals we were picking up in measurement but hadn’t connected the dots. For 11 years, I’ve had low ferritin, without anemia. We continually tried to raise my iron levels with food and supplementation but nothing would work.

We chased the obvious solutions first. A plant-based diet means all my iron is the hard-to-absorb, non-heme kind. Hard training, sauna, and hyperbaric oxygen all raise the body's demand for iron. But none of them explained the core failure: despite me taking iron orally, trialing every formulation, and using every timing trick, none of the iron would stick.

What I didn’t fully appreciate until recently is how many stones my previous providers had left unturned. The low ferritin kept getting explained away but not fixed.

I overhauled my medical team earlier this year. It was the rebuild to lay the groundwork for Immortals Care, our $1M a year protocol. With greater capacity, we revisited everything.

On the surface, my low ferritin was easy to dismiss by most standards of care. My hemoglobin and hematocrit were normal. Ferritin measures stored iron, while hemoglobin measures circulating iron, and because the body drains its reserves first to keep hemoglobin normal, you can be fully iron deficient with a perfectly normal hemoglobin and hematocrit.

This is why my low ferritin kept getting dismissed: the numbers that define anemia looked fine, so no one asked why my iron reserves wouldn't refill.

My team pressed on that question. They first turned to a colonoscopy. I was 48 years old and overdue. It was good health hygiene to have while also serving a specific purpose of searching for a hidden source of blood loss such as a polyp or even cancer in my bowels. Either one of those would be an explanation of why the iron kept disappearing.

At the same time, they began connecting the dots. Iron absorption depends on stomach acid, so one theory was that my stomach acid was disrupted. They also knew that thyroid and stomach autoimmunity often travel together, so often that the pairing has a name: thyrogastric syndrome.

Put against my 27+ year history of autoimmune thyroid disease, the pieces pointed to a single hypothesis: my own immune system was attacking my stomach.

To our surprise, my colonoscopy came back clean. A perfectly healthy colon, better than 95% of colonoscopies of men, according to the gastroenterologist. That ruled out the first concern and worst possible outcome: slow continuous bleeding from colon cancer, or pre-cancerous polyp.

My team had exercised great foresight though, anticipating this possible outcome. In addition to a colonoscopy, they’d ordered an upper endoscopy to be performed at the same time. The combined procedure is a bi-directional endoscopy. Probes would look at my entire intestinal tract, up from below and down the throat.

Additionally, we had several blood biomarkers measured ahead of the procedure to try and pick up on any signals that would give the gastroenterologist guidance for what to look for while doing visual inspections.

Fifteen minutes before the procedure, my blood results returned, finding elevated levels of anti-parietal-cells-antibodies (APCA). They came back at roughly five times the upper limit of normal (103, against a ceiling of 20 Units/mL). It was a positive result confirming the suspicion of AIG being the culprit behind my low ferritin, the other type of gastritis, driven by a bacterial infection, was already ruled out, as we knew I am negative to H. pylori.

Even before this finding, my team had ordered five biopsies to be taken from three regions of my stomach.

The biopsies were the critical piece. Had they not been ordered, the bi-directional endoscopy would have been completed and AIG remained undiagnosed as there were no visual signatures of the condition in my intestines.

Two days later, the results of biopsies came in, showing clear signs of early autoimmune gastritis: early atrophy confined to the acid-producing lining, with the rest of the stomach still spared. My team had anticipated this, methodically tracing every line of evidence.

We now had a formal diagnosis. I have autoimmune gastritis AIG. My stomach is eating itself.

So this was never one problem. It was three, linked to one another: the iron deficiency, the autoimmune gastritis driving it, and the autoimmune thyroid disease alongside it. Iron and thyroid feed each other both ways, low iron impairs the conversion of thyroid hormone into its active form, and an under active thyroid impairs how the body uses iron. Each made the other harder to fix.

Autoimmune gastritis affects an estimated 2–5% of people, and likely more, because it hides and is challenging to diagnose. It's usually silent for years, surfacing only once the stomach has atrophied enough to do real damage: iron deficiency first, then B12 deficiency, then anemia from both, and over a long horizon, raised stomach-cancer risk. In one study of people with precancerous gastric lesions, roughly 18% carried the autoimmune antibodies, and only about 1% had ever been diagnosed.

And the earliest clue, low ferritin, is the one standard medicine waves through. Low iron stores get normalized and rarely investigated at all when anemia hasn't shown up yet. That blind spot is what hid mine for a decade.

The good news: the iron deficiency is now corrected. I received a 1,000 mg Monoferric iron infusion. This was chosen for two reasons after considering multiple formulations. First, it can safely deliver a full dose of iron in a single infusion (1,000 mg), while older options like Venofer require several separate appointments to reach the same total.

Second, certain other IV iron formulations can cause a drop in blood phosphate levels, an important mineral for bones and energy. Monoferric is much less likely to do this, which matters given how closely we track long-term metabolic and bone health parameters.

As mentioned earlier, current medical standards treat AIG as something to be managed, not resolved.

It's worth noting that many of you give me a hard time, inviting me to "live life" and engage in self-destructive behaviors like a "normal person". I'm cool with the playful ribbing. Also, had I not taken care of my health during the past five years, my situation could potentially be very serious.

You too may have a lurking health issue that is undiagnosed and could increase in severity from unhealthy life choices, without your knowing. The absence of symptoms is not the presence of health.

A gentle nudge that minding your health, no matter your situation in life, is good decision making.

My team and I are going to try and solve my AIG. This is how we’re approaching it:

First, routine monitoring keeps the disease in view: ferritin and iron, B12, the pepsinogen I/II ratio, gastrin, and chromogranin A. Gastrin is the dial to watch. If it climbs, the disease is advancing, and the risk of gastric neuroendocrine tumors climbs with it.

Second, we’re doing advanced characterization of the disease. We’ll do a repeat biopsy to read the immune infiltrate, deep cytokine profiling, and T-cell subset analysis, to see which pathways are actually firing.

That testing drives the intervention plan, including the experimental approaches we intend to develop.

+ If gastrin and chromogranin rise: damp the gastrin drive (netazepide) and tighten endoscopic surveillance. If the profile is Th1 / interferon-driven: target JAK/STAT.

+ If it's Th17 / IL-17-driven: target IL-17 and STAT3.

+ If regulatory T cells are failing: rebuild them (low-dose IL-2, induced Tregs).

+ If it's antibody- and B-cell-driven and antigen-specific: engineered cell therapy (CAAR-T).

Which organizes into four tiers, from available today to frontier:

Tier 1, now: protect and support; zinc-L-carnosine, and acid replacement (betaine HCl with pepsin) under physician supervision. This is specific to my case and not something to self-prescribe, especially given the cancer-surveillance considerations above.

Tier 2, target the signaling , JAK/STAT, GSK-3, IL-17, and damp the gastrin drive (netazepide).

Tier 3, reset the cells, induced regulatory T cells (iTregs).

Tier 4, frontier: engineered T-cell therapy (CAR-T / CAAR-T), custom AI-designed antibodies, or synthetic proteins, that can specifically seek out inactivate or destroy the rogue immune cells attacking my stomach lining.

To be clear: there's no approved cure for autoimmune gastritis today. Medicine treats it as something to manage, not solve. Tiers 2 through 4 are investigational preclinical evidence at best, and in several cases therapies that still have to be built.

If you're working on autoimmune gastritis, antigen-specific tolerance, regulatory T cells, or CAAR-T for organ-specific autoimmunity, please reach out.

Modern medicine has normalized too many conditions that erode our health, function, and comfort, shrinking the goal to monitoring and management while a cure is rarely even attempted. Most of these verdicts were handed down decades ago, in an era that predates nearly all of our current tech and science, and they have gone largely unchallenged.

We want to change that. In the age of AI, multiomics, and custom-built DNA, proteins, and cells, no condition should be presumed incurable simply because no one has yet tried to cure it with today's stack.

I’ll end on a personal note.

We fill our days mostly on things that are trivial next to what we ultimately care about. We know, deep down, however, that in the noise of it all, health is easily forgotten until it’s the only thing that matters.

We spend a fraction of our lives truly sober to the preciousness of life. We feel it when someone we love dies, when a child is born, when we come close to death ourselves, or when a diagnosis marks our limit. In those moments, we are sobered, and the rarity of it all becomes self evident. Imagine the existence we’d build together if that clarity didn’t fade.

I wish all of you the very best. Care for yourself, care for others, care for the planet and care for our animal friends. Care for life as it’s the most precious gift there is.

Anti-aging influencer and millionaire Bryan Johnson has recently disclosed that he is battling an autoimmune disease called autoimmune gastritis (AIG). For those unaware, it is a hidden condition in which the immune system attacks the stomach lining. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter), Johnson wrote: “I have an autoimmune disease. My stomach is eating itself.” He explained that the illness often goes undetected, affecting an estimated 2–5% of people, and can lead to nutritional deficiencies, anemia, and elevated cancer risk over time.He also recounted how his health journey began with hypothyroidism, diagnosed at age 21, which he managed with hormone replacement therapy. For over a decade, however, he struggled with low ferritin levels despite normal hemoglobin and hematocrit, a sign of iron deficiency that was repeatedly dismissed by doctors.A recent bi-directional endoscopy and blood tests revealed elevated anti-parietal cell antibodies and biopsy-confirmed early-stage autoimmune gastritis. Johnson noted that his colonoscopy was clear, ruling out hidden bleeding, but the stomach biopsies confirmed the autoimmune attack.Johnson also highlighted the connection between thyroid and stomach autoimmunity, often referred to as thyrogastric syndrome. His case illustrates how iron deficiency, autoimmune gastritis, and thyroid disease can reinforce one another, making treatment more complex.
Article Summary: Bryan Johnson has an autoimmune disease called Autoimmune Gastritis (AIG). AIG causes irreversible damage, nutritional deficiency, anemia, and elevated cancer risk. Johnson's doctors tried to raise his iron levels with food and supplementation but nothing would work. Johnson is the founder of Immortals Care.

Article Title: Americans donated $617.20 billion in the year Elon Musk said that donating money wisely is 'very hard' and biggest challenge I find with my foundation is ...
Article Text:
Cause that American gave donated most to 2025



Elon Musk has repeatedly criticised MacKenzie Scott's donations

Elon Musk spoke about philanthropy on Nikhil Kamath's People by WTF podcast in 2025. Talking about charity, the world's richest man said that he finds that "it’s very difficult to give away money" effectively. Musk added that simply writing checks doesn't ensure the money is used correctly, and emphasized his philosophy that one should focus on creating genuine value for society rather than donating directly. He told Kamath in the podcast that the biggest challenge he finds with his foundation is trying to give money away in a way that is truly beneficial to people. “It’s very easy to give money away to get the appearance of goodness. It is very difficult to give money away for the reality of goodness. Very difficul,.” said Musk.Incidentally, Tesla made his observation in the very year in which US charitable giving reportedly surpassed the $600 billion mark for the first time ever. According to 'Giving USA 2026: The Annual Report on Philanthropy for the Year 2025', donations by individuals, bequests, foundations and corporations to the US charities increased 5.7% in current dollars (3.0% adjusted for inflation) to an estimated $617.20 billion in 2025.'Giving USA: The Annual Report on Philanthropy', which claims to be the longest-running and most comprehensive report on the sources and uses of charitable giving in America, is published every year by Giving USA Foundation, a public service initiative of The Giving Institute. It is researched and written by the Indiana University Lilly Family School of Philanthropy at Indiana University Indianapolis.As per the report, Bequest donations rose nearly 20% (16.6% adjusted for inflation) over 2024, the largest increase of any of the four sources of giving in 2025. Education, public-society benefit, and environment/animals saw more than 10% growth in current dollars. The three types of recipient charities (subsectors) have seen the largest annualized rates of change over the last five years.“U.S. charitable giving exceeded $600 billion in 2025, a milestone that reflects the resilience of American generosity,” said Wendy McGrady, Chair of Giving USA Foundation and President and COO of The Curtis Group. “Amid a volatile economy and ongoing financial pressures for many households, it’s heartening to see generosity at this scale.”“Giving through bequests and by foundations were among the most robust areas for generosity, a continuation of the trends seen in recent years,” said Amir Pasic, Ph. D. , the Eugene R. Tempel Dean of the Indiana University Lilly Family School of Philanthropy. “This likely is in part a reflection of growing asset values due to the strong performance of financial markets in recent years.”Elon Musk has on numerous occasions publicly criticized MacKenzie Scott's donations. World's first trillionaire CEO has reposted or commented approvingly on at least eight posts on Twitter criticizing Scott's giving in the past four days. "Unfortunately, she's spending it on making the world a worse place," another Twitter user posted about Scott's giving. "Sadly, yes," Musk replied.Elon Musk's comments about Scott come amid a fresh wave of criticism of his short-lived Department of Government Efficiency for championing cuts to USAID in 2025. The world's richest man defended the suspension of USAID programs and staff layoffs as an effort to clamp down on waste, fraud, and abuse.
Article Summary: Elon Musk spoke about philanthropy on Nikhil Kamath's People by WTF podcast in 2025. Said that he finds it difficult to give away money effectively. Tesla CEO has repeatedly criticised MacKenzie Scott's donations. US charitable giving reportedly surpassed $600 billion mark for first time ever.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai: "A person who is happy is not because everything is right in his life, he is happy because…"
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai (AI-generated image)

Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai

"A person who is happy is not because everything is right in his life, he is happy because his attitude towards everything in his life is right"

What is the meaning of the quote by Sundar Pichai

From a middle-class home in Chennai to the top of Alphabet

How to apply this quote in daily life



Other famous quotes by Sundar Pichai

"Wear your failure as a badge of honour."

"You might fail a few times, but that's okay. You end up doing something worthwhile which you learn a great deal from."

"In life, don't react, always respond."

"It is always good to work with people who make you feel insecure about yourself. That way, you will constantly keep pushing your limits."

Two people can lose the exact same job on the exact same day and walk away with completely different weeks ahead of them. One spends it replaying every mistake. The other starts updating a CV by evening. Nothing about the actual event changed between them, only what each person decided to do with it. Sundar Pichai , the chief executive of Google and Alphabet, has been credited with putting that idea into words. "A person who is happy is not because everything is right in his life, he is happy because his attitude towards everything in his life is right," he is said to have observed. It is a simple line, but it names something most people never quite stop to notice about their own bad days.The quote separates two things people often treat as the same: the circumstances of a life, and the interpretation placed on those circumstances. Most people assume happiness follows automatically from good outcomes and unhappiness from bad ones, as though the connection were fixed and automatic. This quote argues the connection is not fixed at all. It runs through a filter, and that filter is attitude.This is a harder claim than it first sounds, because it puts a measure of responsibility on the person experiencing difficulty rather than only on the difficulty itself.It is not suggesting that circumstances do not matter or that hardship should be ignored. It is suggesting that two people facing comparable hardship can end up in very different places emotionally, and that the difference has more to do with how each of them processed the event than with the event itself.It is worth being precise about what the quote is not claiming, since ideas like this are easy to stretch too far. It is not arguing that attitude can undo genuine, serious misfortune, or that people experiencing real hardship simply need a better outlook. The claim is narrower and more useful than that. Within the ordinary range of setbacks most people encounter, career disappointments, awkward social situations, plans that fall through, the interpretation applied to the event often shapes the emotional outcome more than the event's objective severity does.Pichai's own life offers a fairly concrete backdrop for a quote about attitude mattering more than circumstance. He grew up in a modest two-room flat in Chennai, India, where his family did not own a car and waited years for a landline telephone connection. He has spoken about sharing a room with his brother and travelling by crowded public bus, describing an upbringing defined far more by constraint than comfort.He went on to study at the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, then Stanford University and the Wharton School, before joining Google in 2004 and eventually becoming chief executive of the company in 2015, later expanding that role to lead its parent company, Alphabet, as well. That trajectory involved plenty of moments where circumstances alone would not have predicted the outcome. A scholarship that almost did not materialise, a family that could not easily afford international travel, and a career built inside one of the most competitive industries in the world all offered repeated opportunities for the story to have gone differently, had attitude not been doing some of the work circumstances alone could not.None of this proves Pichai actually said the words attributed to him. It does suggest why the sentence sticks so easily to his name regardless. A leader whose own biography reads like a case study in outcomes exceeding circumstances makes for a plausible source of a quote insisting exactly that, whether or not he ever put it in precisely those terms himself.Putting this into practice starts with noticing the gap between an event and your reaction to it, since most people move through that gap so quickly they never actually see it happen. A missed promotion, a difficult client, a plan that falls apart at the last minute, all of these register first as facts, and only afterwards as feelings. The feeling is where attitude actually operates, and it is more adjustable than it usually feels in the moment.A useful habit is to separate, out loud or on paper, what actually happened from the story being told about what it means. "I did not get the promotion" is a fact. "I am not good enough for this role" is a story built on top of that fact, and it is the story, not the fact, that usually determines whether the setback becomes a source of growth or a source of lasting discouragement.The gap between what happens and what it means is where most of the real work of living takes place, and most people cross it so quickly they never notice it exists. Slowing down in that gap long enough to choose the interpretation rather than simply inherit it is what the quote is actually asking for, which is harder than it sounds and more available than it feels.
Article Summary: Sundar Pichai is the chief executive of Google and Alphabet. He is said to have said: "A person who is happy is not because everything is right in his life" The quote separates two things people often treat as the same: circumstances and interpretation.

Article Title: After Dell's $6.25 billion Trump Accounts donation, chip giant Micron gifts millions of its own; CEO Sanjay Mehrotra says this is as important as investing in...
Article Text:
What Micron is actually putting donating to Trump Accounts



How Trump Accounts work and who else has signed on



A pledge that lands alongside Micron's bigger US bet



Micron Technology is putting $250 million into Trump Accounts, the government's new savings scheme for American children, days before the program opens for contributions on July 4. President Donald Trump called it the "biggest corporate investment of its kind," praising CEO Sanjay Mehrotra on Truth Social for a move he says will make "millions of children extremely happy" someday. The chipmaker's pledge follows a much larger $6.25 billion donation from Michael and Susan Dell back in December, and signals that corporate America's courtship of the Trump administration now extends well beyond factory announcements and White House dinners.The $250 million breaks into two parts. Micron will match employee contributions dollar-for-dollar, up to $1,000 per child under 18, for workers who want to fund their kids' accounts. Separately, the company will drop a one-time $250 seed deposit into accounts for children living in counties where Micron has operations, spanning Idaho, New York, Virginia, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and Texas. Put together, Micron expects the program to reach up to a million children, with the bulk of the money flowing into communities near its plants and offices.Mehrotra framed it as an extension of the company's existing US footprint. "This investment is about helping children build a strong foundation for future opportunity while supporting the workforce and communities that will shape US semiconductor leadership," he said in a statement, thanking Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent for setting up the accounts in the first place.Trump Accounts were created under last year's tax bill and function like a hybrid of a custodial account and an IRA. Any US citizen child born between January 1, 2025 and December 31, 2028 with a Social Security number gets a one-time $1,000 seed deposit from the federal government. Parents, guardians, and others can add up to $5,000 a year, and employers can chip in pretax contributions of up to $2,500 per employee annually. The money has to sit in low-cost US stock index funds until the child turns 18, at which point the account starts behaving like a traditional IRA, complete with penalties for early withdrawal.Micron isn't the only company writing checks. Nvidia, Goldman Sachs, and Uber have all pledged to match the government's $1,000 seed contribution for employees' children. Bank of New York Mellon is handling the accounts as financial agent, while Robinhood is serving as brokerage and initial trustee, and the two are building a white-label app for Treasury.The Trump Accounts commitment sits on top of Micron's existing promise to invest more than $200 billion in US memory manufacturing and R&D, a build-out the company says will create over 90,000 jobs. It's also throwing hundreds of millions more at semiconductor and AI education programs, from K-12 STEM curricula to community college partnerships and apprenticeships.The timing isn't incidental. Micron's announcement lands right as the tech industry has been visibly cozying up to the White House, from CEOs joining Trump's China trip to companies lining up behind pet initiatives like the Trump Accounts and the new White House ballroom. For Micron, a company that just crossed the $1 trillion market cap mark in May on the back of the AI boom, $250 million is a rounding error with outsized political payoff.
Article Summary: Micron Technology is putting $250 million into Trump Accounts, the government's new savings scheme for American children. President Donald Trump called it the "biggest corporate investment of its kind" Micron expects the program to reach up to a million children, with the bulk of the money flowing into communities near its plants and offices.

Article Title: Xbox has a plan for your disc collection, just as Sony kills physical games
Article Text:
As Sony ditches discs, Xbox tests a way to digitize your games

The feature works the way you'd want it to, mostly

Older games don't make the cut

This is really about the next Xbox

Buy a game, own a game—that used to be the deal. Sony changed it this week, announcing the end of PlayStation disc production after 2028. But the same day, Xbox quietly moved in a different direction, and it might matter more to anyone with a shelf full of cases. Microsoft is testing a feature called "Disc2Digital" that converts your physical games into digital copies you can play without the disc. The Verge reported the details, and what they add up to is clear. The all-digital future is coming fast, but Xbox doesn't want collectors left holding dead plastic.Slot a disc into your Xbox, install the game, and play it while signed into your Microsoft account. That's it. The console reads the disc and hands you a digital copy. No codes, no proof of purchase. References to "enable Disc2Digital" first showed up in the Xbox PC app code in May, and The Verge reports internal testing kicked off soon after.The catch sits in the fine print. Your digital copy is chained to the disc, not your account. Sell the game or lend it to a friend, and the digital version jumps to whoever loads the disc next. Think of it as a physical game wearing a digital coat—you get discless installs, plus cloud streaming and Play Anywhere access across PCs and handhelds when a title supports them.Not everything qualifies. Disc2Digital covers Xbox One and Xbox Series X/S discs only. Original Xbox and Xbox 360 titles are locked out, so those classics stay on the disc or nowhere. Even some Xbox One games might miss the cut—Microsoft told testers that eligibility hinges on how and when a disc was manufactured, and older pressings may lack the data the feature needs.The concept isn't new. Microsoft floated nearly the same idea for the Xbox One back in 2013, then buried it after fans revolted over always-online rules. What's changed is the ground beneath it. Roughly four in five PlayStation games already sell digitally—the market that once rejected this now runs on it.Follow the thread and it leads to Project Helix, Microsoft's next-gen console. The Verge says Microsoft hasn't decided whether it ships with a disc drive, though Windows Central reports the company is leaning toward cutting it—the same road Sony looks set to take with the PS6.If Helix goes disc-free, Disc2Digital stops being a bonus and becomes the bridge. It's the difference between carrying your collection to the new hardware and starting over. Microsoft is running internal tests now, with more expected in the coming months. Whether that's a genuine olive branch to physical fans or just a softer landing into a digital-only world depends on how the final rules shake out.
Article Summary: Microsoft is testing a feature called "Disc2Digital" that converts your physical games into digital copies. The feature works the way you'd want it to, mostly, but older games don't make the cut. Original Xbox and Xbox 360 titles are locked out, so those classics stay on the disc or nowhere.

Article Title: Chip sector group writes letter to treasury secretary Scott Bessent warning ‘risks’ of US policies on memory shortage
Article Text:
The massive AI bottleneck



A semiconductor industry group has issued a warning to the Trump administration, stating that any government attempt to fix the global memory chip shortage by manipulating prices or production will backfire and worsen an already historic supply squeeze. In a letter dated July 1, the SEMI industry association urged US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other top officials to keep their hands off the market, Bloomberg News has reported.The group, which represents global memory giants including Idaho-based Micron Technology, alongside South Korea’s SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, argued that political interventions will only prolong economic pain that the tech industry is currently reeling due to the high prices of memory chips.“While targeted policies can support accelerating domestic supply resilience, interventions that distort pricing or capacity decisions risk prolonging the demand downturn,” SEMI warned in the letter, as per Bloomberg.The letter comes as industries from automotive manufacturing to everyday consumer electronics face an extreme shortage of memory chips. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems require massive amounts of memory to process data streams, and tech giants are buying up every available component to power their advanced AI data centers.While major memory manufacturers expect production capacity to grow by roughly 19% each year, SEMI warned that the explosive demand from AI infrastructure will completely eclipse supply. This leaves a very small number of chips available for consumer goods, and threatens shortages as well as price spikes for cars, laptops and household appliances.The report said that the memory shortage has quickly evolved from a Silicon Valley logistics issue into a major political headache for Washington. While the chip crunch has sent tech stock valuations through the roof, policymakers are deeply worried about voters’ pocketbooks.The financial strain is already hitting consumers. Both Apple and Microsoft have recently hiked prices on popular electronic goods, blaming rising component costs. Moreover, outgoing Apple CEO Tim Cook has reportedly been lobbying Bessent and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for permission to bypass a Pentagon blacklist so Apple can purchase vital memory components from two restricted Chinese suppliers.SEMI opposes any political mandates that dictate who companies can sell to or what they can charge. Instead, the association urged the Trump administration to let tech corporations continue signing private, long-term purchase agreements with their clients.To shield everyday consumers from the rising costs of phones and laptops without damaging the semiconductor supply chain, SEMI pitched a different solution. The group called on the administration to work alongside Congress to pass consumer-focused tax deductions or credits that directly offset the cost of buying personal tech.
Article Summary: SEMI, a semiconductor industry group, has warned the Trump administration against manipulating prices or production. The group argued that political interventions will only prolong economic pain that the tech industry is currently reeling from. The letter comes as industries from automotive manufacturing to everyday consumer electronics face an extreme shortage of memory chips.

Article Title: Quote of the Day by Accenture CEO Julie Sweet: 'You can't get the growth without the skills'
Article Text:
Julie Sweet, CEO, Accenture

Quote of the day by Julie Sweet



What Julie Sweet's quote means



A message reflected in her work



A simple takeaway



Julie Sweet has never been someone who reaches for comfortable abstractions when a direct statement will do. The Chair and CEO of Accenture, one of the world's largest professional services companies with over 700,000 employees across more than 120 countries, has built her leadership reputation on clarity of thought and an unflinching focus on what actually drives results. This quote is a precise example of that quality. It does not gesture toward the importance of learning or suggest that skills are a nice complement to ambition. It states a dependency. Growth without skills is not slower growth. It is not growth at all."You can't get the growth without the skills."The quote is structured as a conditional, and the conditional is absolute. Sweet is not saying skills help growth, or that skilled people tend to grow faster. She is saying the relationship is non-negotiable. You cannot have one without the other. That framing matters because it removes the mental escape hatch that most individuals and organisations quietly rely on, the idea that momentum, vision, or opportunity can carry you forward even when capability has not kept pace.The word "get" is doing more work than it appears to. Growth in Sweet's vocabulary is not passive, it is not something that happens to you if conditions are favourable.You get growth. You go after it, build toward it, and earn it. And the thing that makes you capable of getting it is skills, specifically the right skills for the moment you are in, not the skills that worked a cycle ago.There is also a directional logic embedded in the quote that is easy to miss. Most people think about skills as preparation for growth, something you build in advance of opportunity arriving. Sweet's framing suggests the relationship runs in both directions. Skills do not just enable growth. The pursuit of growth reveals which skills you are missing and forces you to develop them. The two things are not sequential. They are interdependent, each pulling the other forward.For organisations, this has significant strategic implications. A company can set ambitious revenue targets, enter new markets, and acquire competitors, but if the workforce does not have the capabilities to execute in those new contexts, the growth will not stick. Sweet has made this argument publicly in the context of artificial intelligence, arguing repeatedly that the companies falling behind on AI adoption are not failing because of a technology problem. They are failing because of a skills problem.Few CEOs have put skills development as close to the centre of their strategic agenda as Sweet has at Accenture. Under her leadership, the company has invested over a billion dollars annually in training and reskilling its workforce, an extraordinary figure that reflects a genuine institutional belief that human capability is not a fixed resource to be managed but a dynamic one to be continuously developed.Sweet has spoken publicly about the challenge of the AI transition specifically, noting that the speed at which AI is reshaping professional work means that skills built even two or three years ago may already be insufficient for what the next wave of client demands will require. Her response has not been to slow the adoption of AI but to accelerate the investment in the people who need to work alongside it.She has also been candid that this is not purely altruistic. Accenture's business model depends on delivering expertise that clients cannot easily replicate internally. If the skills of its people plateau, so does the value it can deliver, and so does its ability to grow. The quote is, in that sense, a description of Accenture's own operating logic as much as a piece of general wisdom.The quote lands differently depending on where you are in your career. For someone early in their professional life, it is a reminder that ambition without investment in capability is optimism without a plan. For someone mid-career, it is a useful diagnostic: if growth has stalled, the question worth asking is not what opportunities are missing but what skills are. For leaders and organisations, it is a strategic principle with a clear implication. Skills are not a cost centre sitting alongside the growth strategy. They are the growth strategy. Sweet's career, and the company she runs, are the proof of concept.
Article Summary: Julie Sweet is CEO of Accenture, one of the world's largest professional services companies. The quote is structured as a conditional, and the conditional is absolute. Sweet is not saying skills help growth, but that the relationship is non-negotiable.

Slower than expected AI progress

Mouse tracking software review

Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth admitted company did an ‘atrocious’ job by rolling out its new Applied AI division

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg conceded at an internal town hall this week that the company’s sweeping restructuring had not delivered the expected results. According to a report by Reuters, Zuckerberg said the company’s AI agents had not progressed as quickly as anticipated, and that top executives had ‘miscalculated’ the timing of the changes. The restarting announced earlier this year, included laying off about 8,000 employees—roughly 10% of Meta’s global workforce—and reassigning 7,000 staffers to AI-focused teams. The moves were intended to fund Meta’s massive AI infrastructure investments, projected to reach $145 billion in 2026, but have sparked employee pushback and morale concerns.Zuckerberg has also admitted that the “trajectory of agentic development over at least the last four months hasn’t really accelerated in the way that we expected.” He added that while executives were “super optimistic” about tools like Claude Code from Anthropic earlier this year, the company’s bets on AI agents had not yet paid off. Despite the setbacks, Zuckerberg told employees he expects Meta to begin seeing more significant benefits from its AI investments within three to six months.Meta’s Chief Technology Officer Andrew Bosworth also addressed concerns about the company’s controversial mouse-tracking software, which had been paused after reports of sensitive data exposure.Bosworth said a review indicated that no employee data was included in AI training.If reinstated, the program will operate on an opt-in basis, a reversal from April when U.S. employees were told there was no way to opt out. Bosworth said: “For people who are comfortable, that’s great, they can contribute to this kind of great human survey. To people who are not, it is not an issue.”Recently, Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth admitted in a memo to employees that the company did an ‘atrocious’ job by rolling out its new Applied AI division, as reported by Wired. The unit, which was formed in March this year with 6,500 engineers and product managers, was meant to accelerate Meta’s generative AI projects. Instead, workers descend the transition as chaotic, with some calling it ‘a gulag’. Bosworth added that the company undermined trust by failing to explain the vision clearly by destabilising teams via rapid restructuring. The report further added that Bosworth pledged to rekindle a more cheerful internal culture by improving communication, career growth opportunities, and even office perks. Managers will be capped at 20 direct reports, employees will have access to “AI coaching” tools, and Meta will invest in microkitchens, travel budgets, and social events to boost morale. “I hope we can rekindle the best of the culture we joined,” Bosworth wrote.Meta laid off about 10% of its workforce, or roughly 8,000 employees in May, as part of its ongoing restructuring. The job cuts, combined with broader AI-related organisational changes, have contributed to growing internal unrest across the company.
Article Summary: CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company’s AI agents had not progressed as quickly as anticipated, and that top executives had ‘miscalculated’ the timing of the changes. Article Text:
US Court orders Chinese billionaire to forfeit $889 million

From Chinese property tycoon to US-based political activist

Chinese businessman Guo Wengui, who once joined US President Donald Trump 's Mar-a-Lago golf club in Florida, has been sentenced to 30 years in an American prison. Guo, who was previously regarded as one of China's wealthiest entrepreneurs, was jailed for running what prosecutors described as a billion-dollar cryptocurrency and investment fraud scheme for his online followers. A federal court in New York also ordered him to forfeit $889 million and pay restitution after he was convicted on multiple charges, including racketeering, fraud and money laundering.According to a BBC report, prosecutors alleged that Guo raised more than $1 billion between 2018 and 2023 through investment and cryptocurrency ventures promoted to his online followers. Authorities said the money funded expenses, including a 50,000-square-foot mansion, a $1 million Lamborghini, a $37 million yacht and other luxury purchases. Previously, the New York Times reported that Wengui was a member of the Mar-a-Lago club and was photographed at the Florida resort in March 2017.US District Judge Analisa Torres sentenced Guo in Manhattan, saying he had targeted supporters of his anti-Chinese Communist Party movement and used investor funds to finance a luxury lifestyle. She said he "preyed on those seeking to bring Democracy to China," taking their money so he could live lavishly.The judge also said Guo "takes no responsibility for his actions and instead insists, incredibly, his conduct caused no loss and harmed no one,” another AP report noted.Guo, who is also known as Miles Guo and Ho Wan Kwok, was convicted on nine of 12 criminal charges following a seven-week trial. Prosecutors had argued that the fraud affected more than 1,000 victims worldwide and caused hundreds of millions of dollars in losses.During sentencing, Judge Torres read victim statements describing financial losses, anxiety and damaged family relationships. One victim, Wei Chen, told the court that Guo's fraud "destroyed my life" and that of the victim's family.The court ordered Guo to forfeit $889 million and pay restitution as part of the sentence.Before leaving China, Guo built his fortune as a property developer and maintained business ties with Chinese authorities. He relocated to the United States in 2017 after Chinese officials accused him of corruption, allegations he has denied.In the US, Guo became a critic of the Chinese Communist Party and built a large online following. He also developed ties with former Trump adviser Steve Bannon. In 2020, the two announced the New Federal State of China, a political campaign aimed at opposing China's ruling Communist Party.Before his arrest in 2023, Guo lived in a luxury apartment overlooking Central Park and had become a member of President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club in Florida.Speaking in court before sentencing, Guo defended his intentions. He said,”The reason I came to the U.S. was to destroy the CCP.”Guo's lawyer, Melinda Sarafa, said the 30-year sentence is "excessive" and confirmed that he plans to appeal both his conviction and sentence, maintaining that he did not defraud investors. Meanwhile, China's Foreign Ministry said Guo remains wanted by Chinese authorities and is the subject of an Interpol Red Notice.
Article Summary: Chinese businessman Guo Wengui has been sentenced to 30 years in an American prison. A federal court in New York also ordered him to forfeit $889 million and pay restitution after he was convicted on multiple charges, including racketeering, fraud and money laundering. Prosecutors alleged that Guo raised more than $1 billion through investment and cryptocurrency ventures promoted to his online followers.
